summary: Overt action complements occur with d- (Lahdo Traitor 2/21), without d- (MAC Farida/93), or remain understood (JL 6.10/3). Preterit L-endings and Infectum subject endings encode the person who dares; complement objects belong to the dependent verb.
m- identifies a feared person or inhibiting authority (75/224; 67/127; 98/68), already compatible with sense 1. It does not establish a separate object sense.

Negated Infectum can describe a past scene without -wa (JL 8.11/14), while Infectum-wa occurs in past descriptions and rhetorical questions. Maǧrútuwa (MAC Hanna Dewo/233) alone does not distinguish past from irrealis force.
Several German editions use können or vermögen for maǧr- (PrS 35/66; 59/14; 80/15); the Turoyo does not establish a distinct ability sense. Ordinary daring remains the conservative analysis.

Read-only lookup of ǧrʕ confirms the same Arabic etymology and an internally questioned III ko-maǧrono example (MM 57), alongside a distinct II paradigm. Reconciliation needs editorial review; no existing example is moved.

All full records support III.1. Compact records omit verses; their classifications remain provisional and contribute no quotations. Repeated tokens remain separate ledger lines; already cited passages, including JL 19.6/13, 43/34 and 69/516, are not added again.

All 30 occurrences support inherited III.1 sich trauen, wagen. Fear, threats, law, family inhibition and political constraints explain the modal judgement without creating separate ability or permission senses.

Round 1 leaves five Preterit examples, eight Infectum examples and five Infectum-wa examples. Reader thin-cell counts refer to the original entry; no further routine example is needed. No new box, sense, idiom or correction is warranted.

Jan 4.II/879 me man asks for the source of inhibition; it continues the m-complement pattern already noted in R1. kmaǧrən versus kmaǧri in adjacent discussion is a form/agreement observation, not a new stem.

Frequent first-person plural forms occur in social and political discussion; the experiencer controls the dependent action. Bare complements can retain -wa (maǧrewo muḥewo) or appear without it (maǧralle d fayši).
